newsitem.title: MEXICO: New Mexico City mayor to scrap army's police role.
newsitem.headline: New Mexico City mayor to scrap army's police role.

text.p: Left-wing mayor-elect Cuauhtemoc Cardenas plans to scrap a controversial policy of militarizing Mexico City's corrupt police force when he takes over later this year, his aides said on Wednesday.

Some 3,000 soldiers have taken on police work in different neighbourhoods of the city while their civilian counterparts are sent on two-month military training courses in an effort to root out corruption and inefficiency.
Although the programme was billed as temporary, scores of soldiers have spent months on the job to fill in for hundreds of police who failed their military training course.

"The troops will return to the barracks, where they belong," said Raul Breton, a high-ranking member of the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) and an advisor to Cardenas, who takes office in December.
Breton told Reuters Cardenas plans to offer civilian police higher salaries to stop corruption and encourage them to denounce their superiors engaged in crooked practices.
Cardenas handily won the first Mexico City mayor race in July 6 mid-term elections, handing the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) its worst electoral defeat.

Even though police receive training on joining the force, they are corrupted by their superiors as soon as they begin active duty, Breton said. Such practices include bribing their superior officers for the right to extort civilians or motorists at strategic points across the city.

Officials eager to stamp out a crime wave say residents who have seen the soldiers like them and want to keep the programme. But police have denounced the threat to their jobs, staging violent protests in May in which dozens were injured.
Many leftists worry that the military's takeover of civilian policing duties in the capital is an ominous sign of a growing militarization of the country as a whole.

Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo has replaced hundreds of state policemen and policewomen with army troops in the past year and given the army the task of fighting the multi-billion dollar illegal drug trade passing through Mexico.
